Seasonal lag (thermal inertia): Earth's oceans, land and atmosphere absorb and store heat, so temperatures respond slowly to solar input. Winter solstice marks minimum insolation (shortest day, lowest sun angle), but net heat loss continues until incoming solar energy exceeds outgoing longwave radiation. Coldest period typically occurs about 4–6 weeks later, in late January or February in the Northern Hemisphere.

Specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise a substance's temperature, is far higher for water than for land, so oceans store more heat and release it slowly. Wave breaking depends on wave height, wavelength, water depth, and steepness. As waves move into shallower water, wave speed and wavelength decrease while wave height increases (shoaling), so steepness grows. At constant frequency (period), wavelength shrinks with depth, and the wave eventually becomes unstable when height exceeds about 0.78 times water depth, causing plunging, spilling, or surging breakers.
